content: 1. A robust governance framework for value-based pricing, utilizing health technology assessment (HTA), has been established to ensure transparency in processes. Assessment reports and decisions are made publicly available to maintain accountability. 2. The methodology and perspective for determining value in healthcare are explicitly defined. Decisions and evidence are subject to periodic review and reassessment to ensure relevance and accuracy. 3. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) acknowledged the limited evidence from comparative studies that meet the standards of the WHO-commissioned systematic review. While the overall balance of effects favors value-based pricing, the GDG emphasized that outcomes are likely to vary significantly depending on the robustness of value assessment through HTA. 4. The GDG cautioned that unconstrained value-based pricing could result in unaffordable prices, potentially jeopardizing the sustainability of health systems. 5. Implementing best-practice value-based pricing using HTA presents significant feasibility challenges, particularly in health systems lacking the necessary financial and human resources to manage the governance and technical complexities of this policy option. 6. Evidence from systematic reviews indicates that pricing or decision-making processes based on value, as determined through HTA, are likely to yield more desirable than undesirable effects. This is supported by theoretical rationale, limited evidence of adverse effects, and widespread adoption of value-based pricing as a primary or supporting pricing policy. 7. However, the effectiveness of value-based pricing depends on the capacity of health systems to manage the technical and procedural complexities associated with HTA. 8. The generalizability of findings from systematic reviews is unclear, as most evidence originates from high-income countries and often focuses on a limited subset of medicines with methodological shortcomings. 9. The concept and approach of value-based pricing and HTA have gained attention and some acceptance among governments, particularly in higher-income countries. However, the significant human and financial resources required for institutionalizing HTA and formalizing value-based pricing may pose barriers to broader acceptance. 10. Patients and communities may object to pricing or reimbursement decisions that fail to fully capture social values or judgments on social equity. 11. Value-based pricing informed by HTA requires substantial human and financial resources to manage the technical, administrative, and governance aspects of implementation. It is data-intensive, necessitating robust IT infrastructure and reliable data. 12. The feasibility of implementing value-based pricing varies depending on existing capacity, including data availability, to conduct value assessments through HTA. Many new medicines lack well-established evidence to inform their clinical and economic value at the time of regulatory and reimbursement approvals, posing challenges even in countries with established HTA authorities. 13. Existing health systems in high-income countries that utilize value-based pricing through HTA suggest that, once established and with timely reforms, such institutions and processes are sustainable. However, the financial implications of this approach compared to alternative policies remain unclear. 14. Effective implementation of value-based pricing using HTA should aim to maximize health outcomes. Countries should tailor approaches to local decision-making structures and technical capacity, collaborate to exchange information, and develop common requirements where appropriate. 15. Legislative and administrative frameworks for value-based pricing using HTA should clearly define the roles and responsibilities of decision-makers and stakeholders, as well as the decision-making process. 16. Horizon scanning may be conducted to anticipate future medicines and technologies, particularly those with significant public health impacts. 17. Mark-up regulation in the pharmaceutical supply chain involves controlling additional charges applied to medicine prices to cover overhead costs, distribution charges, and profit margins. This policy aims to reduce price variability along the supply chain, enhance price transparency, and provide predictability for expenditure management. 18. Mark-up regulation is commonly used in many healthcare systems to set price and mark-up thresholds across the pharmaceutical supply chain. Examples include South Africa’s single exit price regulation and WHO recommendations for regressive mark-up structures. 19. The GDG emphasized that well-designed mark-up regulation is essential to avoid undesirable effects, such as price convergence toward maximum regulated prices or supplier-induced demand for products with higher mark-up margins. 20. Effective operation of mark-up regulations requires adequate expertise, mechanisms for monitoring medicine prices and sales, and consideration of potential effects on non-regulated products and health service revenues. 21. Price transparency involves sharing and disclosing information on pharmaceutical prices to relevant parties and the public to ensure accountability. This includes details on production costs, R&D costs, therapeutic value, and profit margins. 22. Price transparency is critical for designing and implementing pricing policies. Non-transparent medicine prices can conflict with principles of good governance and compromise accountability. 23. Several countries have implemented measures to promote price transparency, such as mandatory public disclosure of list prices for reimbursable medicines in the European Union.
